lessons.title: Substitutions for People and Roles
lessons.concept: One-word substitution replaces a phrase describing a person, habit, or role with a single precise word. These questions test vocabulary and understanding of common descriptive phrases.
lessons.formula: Approach: understand the key meaning of the phrase -> recall or identify the single word that best represents it.
lessons.worked_example: Phrase: 'A person who does not believe in God' -> Atheist. Phrase: 'A person who loves mankind' -> Philanthropist (in broad usage; in common aptitude contexts, 'philanthropist' refers to one who helps others, but check options carefully). A clearer example: 'A person who is unable to read or write' -> Illiterate.
mistakes: Choosing a word with related meaning but not exact substitution
Ignoring the specific scope of the phrase

lessons.title: Substitutions for Places and Things
lessons.concept: Many substitutions describe places, objects, or conditions using a single noun or adjective. Focus on the defining characteristic in the phrase (where, what purpose, what quality).
lessons.formula: Identify defining feature (location/purpose/quality) -> match to precise term.
lessons.worked_example: Phrase: 'A place where books are kept' -> Library. Phrase: 'That which cannot be heard' -> Inaudible.
mistakes: Picking a general term instead of the specific one
Confusing place-based terms (e.g., library/museum/archive) when phrase is specific
Selecting an adjective when a noun is required by meaning (or vice versa)

lessons.title: Substitutions for Actions and Qualities
lessons.concept: Some phrases describe actions, time periods, or qualities that can be expressed in one word (e.g., something that happens every year -> annual). Pay attention to time/frequency, possibility, and manner implied in the phrase.
lessons.formula: Check modifiers like 'cannot be', 'every', 'one who' -> map to precise word form (impossible/inevitable, annual, etc.).
lessons.worked_example: Phrase: 'That which cannot be avoided' -> Inevitable. Phrase: 'A life story written by oneself' -> Autobiography.
mistakes: Confusing 'cannot be avoided' (inevitable) with 'cannot be solved' (insolvable)
Mixing up biography (written by someone else) and autobiography (by oneself)
